overview.headline: How opposition to Constitution led to proposal and ratification of Bill of Rights

keyPoints.point: amendments were originally proposed and ratified became Bill of Rights
keyPoints.quote: Although 12 amendments were originally proposed, the 10 that were ratified became the Bill of Rights in 1791.

keyPoints.point: opponents repeatedly charged Constitution would open way to tyranny by central government
keyPoints.quote: its opponents repeatedly charged that the Constitution as drafted would open the way to tyranny by the central government

keyPoints.point: citizens demanded bill of rights to spell out immunities of individual citizens
keyPoints.quote: They demanded a "bill of rights" that would spell out the immunities of individual citizens.

keyPoints.point: First Congress proposed amendments to Constitution for state legislatures to consider
keyPoints.quote: the First Congress of the United States therefore proposed to the state legislatures 12 amendments to the Constitution

keyTerms.gloss: proposed changes to Constitution that were originally proposed as formal additions
keyTerms.quote: Although 12 amendments were originally proposed, the 10 that were ratified became the Bill of Rights in 1791.

keyTerms.gloss: oppressive rule by central government feared if Constitution opened way to abuse
keyTerms.quote: its opponents repeatedly charged that the Constitution as drafted would open the way to tyranny by the central government

keyTerms.gloss: protections that spell out rights of individual citizens against government action
keyTerms.quote: They demanded a "bill of rights" that would spell out the immunities of individual citizens.

keyTerms.gloss: formally approved by state legislatures after being proposed by Congress
keyTerms.quote: Articles 3 to 12, ratified December 15, 1791, by three-fourths of the state legislatures
